title: Interfaces, inheritance & polymorphism
summary: virtual and override versus new, abstract and sealed, interfaces with default and explicit members, base calls, and programming against interfaces so implementations can be swapped and tested.
lesson:
## Interfaces: contracts

```csharp
public interface IEmailSender
{
    Task SendAsync(string to, string subject, string body);
}
public class SmtpEmailSender : IEmailSender { ... }
public class FakeEmailSender : IEmailSender { public List<string> Sent { get; } = new(); ... }
```

Code that depends on `IEmailSender` works with any implementation: SMTP in production, a fake in tests, a queue later. That is the core of dependency injection (topic 15). A class can implement many interfaces but inherit from one base class.

Interfaces can carry **default implementations** (C# 8): a member with a body that implementers may skip. They are visible only through the interface type. **Explicit implementation** (`string ILabel.Label() => ...`) hides a member from the class's own surface; it is callable only through the interface.

## Inheritance and virtual dispatch

```csharp
class Animal { public virtual string Speak() => "..."; }
class Dog : Animal { public override string Speak() => "woof"; }

Animal a = new Dog();
a.Speak();   // "woof": the RUNTIME type decides (virtual dispatch)
```

- `virtual` allows overriding; `override` replaces it in a subclass; `base.Speak()` calls the parent's version.
- `abstract` members have no body and must be overridden; an `abstract class` cannot be instantiated.
- `sealed` stops further inheritance (`sealed class`) or further overriding (`sealed override`).
- Members are **non-virtual by default** in C#, unlike Java.

## new is hiding, not overriding

```csharp
class Animal { public string Name() => "animal"; }
class Dog : Animal { public new string Name() => "dog"; }

Animal a = new Dog();
a.Name();          // "animal"  <- chosen by the STATIC (declared) type
((Dog)a).Name();   // "dog"
```

`new` creates an unrelated method that happens to share the name; which one runs depends on the variable's declared type. It is almost always a mistake (forgotten `virtual`); the compiler warns when you hide without saying `new`.

## Type checks

`if (shape is Circle c)` (pattern) and `shape as Circle` (null on failure) test runtime types. If you find yourself switching on types everywhere, a virtual method on the base type is often the cleaner design; when the set of types is closed and the logic lives outside them (mapping results to HTTP codes), pattern matching is fine (topic 04).

## Composition over inheritance

Inheritance couples a subclass to the internals of its parent ("fragile base class"). Prefer small interfaces and composition: a `PriceCalculator` that takes a list of `IDiscountRule` objects is easier to extend and test than a hierarchy of `DiscountedOrder : Order` subclasses. Use inheritance for genuine is-a relationships with a stable base: framework base classes (`ControllerBase`, `BackgroundService`, `DbContext`), exceptions, and abstract templates.

## Liskov in one sentence

A subclass must work wherever its base class is expected: no stronger preconditions, no surprising exceptions. A `ReadOnlyList : List` that throws on `Add` breaks every caller written against `List`.

quiz.prompt: `Animal a = new Dog();` where Dog overrides the virtual `Speak()`. What does `a.Speak()` run?
choices: Animal's Speak, because a is typed Animal
Dog's override
Animal's, then Dog's
It does not compile
quiz.explanation: Virtual dispatch uses the runtime type of the object, not the declared type of the variable.

quiz.prompt: `Dog` declares `public new string Name()` hiding Animal's non-virtual `Name()`. What does `((Animal)new Dog()).Name()` return?
choices: `"dog"`
`"animal"`
It throws InvalidCastException
A compile error
quiz.explanation: Hiding with new binds by the static type: through an Animal reference, Animal's method runs.

quiz.prompt: In C#, are methods virtual by default?
choices: Yes: instance methods are virtual, as in Java
Yes for public methods, no for private ones
No: overriding needs virtual or abstract
No: overriding needs the new modifier instead
quiz.explanation: C# methods are non-virtual unless declared virtual, abstract or override.

quiz.prompt: How do you call the parent's implementation from an override?
choices: `super.Speak()`
`this.Speak()`
`Animal.Speak()`
`base.Speak()`
quiz.explanation: base refers to the immediate parent's members.

quiz.prompt: Where is a default interface method callable?
choices: Only through a reference of the interface type
Directly on any implementing class instance
Only from inside the interface's own other members
Only through base.Method() in the implementing class
quiz.explanation: Default members are not inherited into the class's own surface; cast to the interface to call them.

quiz.prompt: What does `sealed` on a class do?
choices: Makes its instances immutable once created
Makes its members static, like a static class
Prevents other classes from inheriting from it
Prevents it from being instantiated directly
quiz.explanation: sealed stops inheritance; abstract is the one that prevents instantiation.

quiz.prompt: Why do services depend on `IEmailSender` rather than `SmtpEmailSender`?
choices: Interface calls are faster than calls on a concrete class
So implementations can be swapped without changing the service
The DI container cannot register concrete classes
The compiler requires constructor parameters to be interfaces
quiz.explanation: Programming against an interface decouples the caller from one concrete implementation, so a fake in tests or another provider later can be swapped in without touching the service.

choices: Sharing a logging helper between two classes that are otherwise unrelated
Adding retry behaviour to every service through a shared base class
A genuine is-a relationship with a stable base, like BackgroundService
Reusing two utility methods from a class in another module
quiz.explanation: Use composition for sharing behaviour; extend stable framework bases for true specialisation.

quiz.prompt: A `ReadOnlyList` subclass of `List<T>` throws on `Add`. Which principle does it break?
choices: Liskov substitution principle
Single responsibility principle
Interface segregation principle
The open/closed principle of SOLID
quiz.explanation: Callers written against the base type would fail; expose IReadOnlyList<T> instead. The subclass cannot be used everywhere a List is expected.

quiz.prompt: What does `shape as Circle` return when shape is a Square?
choices: A Circle with default values
It throws InvalidCastException
The Square, unchanged
null, with no exception
quiz.explanation: as returns null on failure; an explicit cast (Circle)shape would throw.

flashcards.back: override replaces a virtual member and is chosen by the runtime type; new hides a member and is chosen by the declared type of the variable.

flashcards.front: Are C# methods virtual by default?
flashcards.back: No. Without virtual, abstract or override, a method is resolved at compile time and cannot be overridden.
abstract members must be overridden and abstract classes cannot be created; sealed stops further inheritance or overriding.

flashcards.front: What is a default interface member?
flashcards.back: An interface method with a body that implementers may skip; it is reachable only through the interface type.
Implementing a member as InterfaceName.Member so it is callable only through the interface, not on the class.

flashcards.front: Why depend on interfaces in services?
flashcards.back: The implementation can change, be decorated or be faked in tests without touching the code that uses it.
A subtype must be usable anywhere its base type is, without callers noticing a difference in contract.

flashcards.front: When is type switching a smell?
flashcards.back: When behaviour that belongs to the types is scattered in switches; a virtual method usually fits better unless the set of types is closed.

drills.title: Polymorphic notifiers
drills.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Notifications go out by email and by SMS. The sender loops over a list of notifiers and must not know which kind each one is."

**Why it matters.** An abstract base with virtual members lets one loop drive different behaviour. Overrides can reuse the base logic with `base` and add their own rules.

**Your task.** In the types section, complete the two subclasses of `Notifier`:
- `EmailNotifier`: `Channel` is `"email"`; it keeps the base `Format` unchanged
- `SmsNotifier`: `Channel` is `"sms"`; its `Format` takes the BASE format of the message and, if that is longer than 30 characters, cuts it to 29 characters and appends `…` (so the result is exactly 30 characters)

The base `Format(message)` returns `[channel] message`.

**Worked example.** For the message "Order 42 shipped", the email notifier formats `[email] Order 42 shipped`, and the SMS notifier `[sms] Order 42 shipped`.
hints: The base class already knows how to format; the SMS notifier should reuse it and only apply its length rule.
Override the channel in each subclass, and in the SMS notifier start from the base class's formatted text and shorten it only when it is over the limit.
Give each subclass its channel name, and in the SMS one start from the parent's formatted text, keeping it as it is when it fits and otherwise keeping the first 29 characters followed by an ellipsis.
